findings.element: states.day — render-b.js:1119-1138 (.b-dayWrap holding .b-who/.b-dayCount/.b-dayDate/.b-dayRule/.b-dayNote, then section.b-dayNow, then foot({stamp:false})), plus the dayOf branch at render-b.js:306. Driven at ?v=approach&state=day at 390, 768, 1280 and 1440.
findings.problem: The screen the whole company is judged by is the only guest surface that leaves what the day is out of its head, and it is the only one that will not say when it was last changed. Measured at 390: 206 characters, docH 844, one focusable element. Every other guest surface builds its head from the locked order — .b-horizon children on ?state=phone are exactly b-who, b-count, b-when, b-sub, and b-sub is "Wedding day at The Orchard". On the day that fourth slot is spent on p.b-dayNote "This is the day the plan was for.", a sentence that repeats the 148px word directly above it, and the subject is demoted below a rule into section.b-dayNow under an h2 reading "Happening now". That h2 is a condition label, which the lock retired from this direction by name, and it is false at granularity: with exactly one item beneath it, it reads identically at 07:00 and at 23:00, so it is a label on a list of one that never changes. Then foot({stamp:false}) at line 1136 deletes the "Updated 15 July 2026" stamp that phone, desk, print and all three record rooms carry — on the one morning when whether the plan moved overnight is the only thing a guest is actually worried about. And render-b.js:306 renames the past object from "Behind you" to "How you got here" on this screen alone, so the same guest, on the same phone, meets one object under two names weeks apart. Four separate information defects on 206 characters. The gate cannot see any of them: it asserts the day names where to be, names what is happening, does not claim to be over and is not a counter that ran out — all true, and all satisfied by the arrangement above.
findings.fix: (1) render-b.js:1129 — delete p.b-dayNote and the div.b-dayRule above it, and render in their place h("p.b-sub", { text: todayItems[0].title + " at The Orchard" }) from the accessor states.day already holds, so the day's head reads Mara & Finn / Today / Saturday 3 October 2026 / Wedding day at The Orchard: the same count-date-subject order every other guest surface keeps. (2) Delete section.b-dayNow and its h2 entirely (render-b.js:1131-1134) and the .b-dayNow and .b-dayNowTitle rules at b.css:930-931; the subject now lives in the head, so the condition label has nothing left to caption. (3) render-b.js:1136 — change foot({ stamp: false }) to foot({}), so the morning states its own freshness like every other guest surface. (4) render-b.js:306 — drop the dayOf ternary and always render "Behind you", so the object is named once across the product. (5) Use the band reclaimed by (1) and (2) to promote the keeper out of the 11px mono footer: render h("p.b-daySub", { text: "Kept by " + F.workspace.owner + "." }) beneath the head at the .b-sub treatment, so the person to ask is legible at arm's length. Gate: assert the day's head contains the day's subject string; assert the day's footer text contains "Updated"; assert no element on the day matches /happening now/i; assert the past label string is byte-identical on ?state=day and ?state=phone.

findings.element: a.b-unfurl — render-b.js:1046-1057. Rendered at ?state=unfurl and again on ?state=publish under "What lands in the message". Driven at 390, 768 and 1440; the card is 300x221 at every width.
findings.problem: The card's display line is F.toDay() — the literal string "79" — with "days to Saturday 3 October 2026" beneath it. A chat unfurl is a cached preview: the receiving app fetches it once and keeps the copy. So the artifact that reaches the most people, and the only artifact in the chain the reader cannot refresh, is built around the single value in the fixture guaranteed to be wrong within a day of sending. Open that thread in September and the card says 79 while the page behind it says 14. The publish screen sells exactly this — "It carries the day, the distance and the plan" — and the sender's bubble on ?state=unfurl says "It updates itself". The page does. The card cannot. Two more faults in the same 300px: the couple's name is printed twice, as p.b-ogWho "Mara & Finn" and again as p.b-unfurlTitle "Mara & Finn, a wedding timeline", which spends the card's only prose slot on a duplicate plus a product noun, for an audience defined as someone who has never used a project-management tool and never will — while "Wedding day at The Orchard", the string that says what the thing actually is, appears nowhere on the card. And the aria-label at render-b.js:1046 is "Mara & Finn, a wedding timeline", which on an anchor overrides its contents: a screen-reader user in a chat app is read the title and nothing else, with the count and the date deleted from the accessible name. The gate's "every visible interactive element has an accessible name" passes on the very label that removes them.
findings.fix: (1) render-b.js:1050-1051 — swap the two lines' roles so the card leads with the fact that cannot age: render h("p.b-ogNum", { text: F.fmt.longYear(F.project.primaryDate.date) }) as the display line and h("p.b-ogDate", { text: F.toDay() + " days away when this was sent" }) beneath it. The count keeps its meaning and stops being a claim the cache will falsify. (2) render-b.js:1055 — replace the .b-unfurlTitle text with the day's own subject from the accessor the guest head already uses, so the line reads "Wedding day at The Orchard"; the couple's name stays on b-ogWho and is not printed twice. (3) render-b.js:1046 — delete the aria-label. The card's own contents read as "Mara & Finn, Saturday 3 October 2026, Wedding day at The Orchard, timeline.signalstudio.ie", which is a better name than the one being substituted. If a label is kept it must contain every visible line. Gate: assert a.b-unfurl carries no aria-label, or that its accessible name contains the date; assert the card's text contains the day's subject and contains the couple's name exactly once; assert the card's display-step element is not the day count.

findings.element: p.b-behindNote — render-b.js:329, styled at b.css:437, rendered as a sibling AFTER details.b-behindDetails and therefore never hidden by it.
findings.problem: The round-3 fix that made the record room and the keepsake list the past left behind the sentence that existed to stand in for the list, so wherever the past is listed the same fact is now printed twice, in two grammars, on the same page. Driven and measured: ?v=record&state=desk, ?v=record&state=print, ?v=record&state=phone, ?v=approach&state=print and ?v=paper&state=print all render the rows ["Fri 2 Jan · We said yes", "Sat 18 Apr · The Orchard reserved", "City hotel shortlist · Not going ahead"] and, immediately beneath them, a visible p.b-behindNote reading "The Orchard reserved, 18 April. The city hotel shortlist is not going ahead." The keepsake — the object that sits on a table on the morning — prints "Sat 18 Apr The Orchard reserved" and then "The Orchard reserved, 18 April." about twenty pixels below it. The same happens the moment anyone opens the disclosure: on ?state=day the list ends "Sat 19 Sep Venue walk-through" and the note underneath says "Venue walk-through, 19 September."; on ?state=phone the note repeats two of the three rows above it. This is the library's one-grammar-per-fact class returning through a fix, which is the way it always returns. The gate has assertions that the rows appear; it has none that the summary sentence goes away when the thing it summarises is on screen.
findings.fix: render-b.js:329 — the note must render only while the fold is actually folding. Pass the resolved past decision into behindBlock the same way the rows already read it, and return null for h("p.b-behindNote") when past === "listed"; that covers the record room, print and the paper room. For the folded rooms, add one rule at b.css:437: details.b-behindDetails[open] ~ .b-behindNote { display: none } — the note is already the details element's next sibling, so no markup moves and no layout shifts above it. Gate: assert that on ?v=record no .b-behindNote element exists at desk, print or phone; assert that on ?v=approach&state=print no .b-behindNote element exists; assert that on ?v=approach&state=phone the note is visible with the disclosure closed and fails checkVisibility once the summary is pressed; and assert that no substring of a rendered .b-behindNote matches any .b-behindTitle on the same page.

findings.element: states.ended — render-b.js:1164 onward. Driven at 390 and 1440.
findings.problem: 202 characters, zero focusable elements, and three sentences that all answer the same question. "This link has been turned off." / "The plan for Mara & Finn is no longer shared here. Orla can send a new link whenever they want to." / "Nothing has been deleted. Only the link stopped working." A guest reaches this screen because a link they were sent has stopped working, and a real proportion of them reach it on the morning itself, standing outside a venue. The only question they have is whether the day is still on. The screen never mentions the day at all — no date, no subject, nothing but the couple's name — so a guest is left to infer the worst from a screen that spends every one of its three sentences reassuring them about the link. Second, it asserts a cause it cannot know: the state is named "revoked or expired", and "has been turned off" plus "Orla can send a new link" tells a guest that a named person deliberately cut off their access, which for a link that reached its expiry date is false and reads as being uninvited to a wedding. Third, the one h1 on the screen is "Signal Timeline", so the product's name is the entire heading outline and the message itself is a paragraph — on the only guest surface that is nothing but a message. The gate checks that it says what happened, names who can fix it and says nothing was deleted; all three pass on exactly this copy.
findings.fix: (1) Make the message the heading: change the h1 from "Signal Timeline" to the message line, and move "Signal Timeline" into the footer.b-foot treatment the other guest surfaces already use. (2) Stop asserting a cause the state cannot distinguish: change the message to "This link has stopped working." and "Orla can send a new link whenever they want to." to "Orla can send a new one." — true whether it was revoked or expired. (3) Add one sentence, immediately before "Nothing has been deleted", that answers the question the guest actually arrived with and reveals nothing the link was hiding: "This says nothing about the day itself." Gate: assert the ended screen's single h1 is the message and does not equal the product name; assert its body text contains no phrase attributing the change to a person; assert its body text contains a sentence naming the day.

findings.element: states.loading — render-b.js:1180-1200, the four div.b-skel bars; b.css:962. Measured at 390 against ?state=phone at 390.
findings.problem: The comment above these bars says they are "sized to the real objects they stand for", and their heights are right — 17/83/26/23 against a real 15/86/26/23. Their widths are all width:100%. Measured: the count's real ink is 107x86 at x=17; its placeholder is 346x83 at x=22. The heaviest object in the composition — the number that is the entire product — is promised as a full-bleed slab and delivered as a numeral less than a third that wide, and the same overstatement applies to the other three bars, since the couple's name, the date and the subject are all shorter than the measure. The load therefore ends with the page's mass collapsing rather than resolving, which is the opposite of what a skeleton exists to do. Second, the frame stops at 350px while the arrived phone document is 1674px, so a guest watches the page nearly quintuple in height on arrival with nothing at all reserved below the today line. The comment's defence covers the part it is about — tick positions come from the dates and must not be invented, and that is correct — but it does not cover the parts of the measure whose geometry is not a date: the "Days away" column heading and the spine rule sit in the same place on every plan that will ever load here.
findings.fix: (1) render-b.js:1192-1195 — replace width:100% on each bar with the proportion of the measure its real ink occupies at 390: 32% for the name bar, 31% for the count bar (107/346), 66% for the date bar and 72% for the subject bar. Keep every height as it is. (2) After the today label, reserve the measure's band using only objects that no date determines: the "Days away" column heading in its real treatment, the spine rule at its real x, and exactly one div.b-skel row at the first row's real geometry (x 132, width 236, height 42). Render no .b-tick element and no date-shaped text, so "the loading frame invents no measure" continues to hold on its own terms. (3) Gate: assert no .b-skel has a computed width equal to its container's width; assert the loading frame renders zero .b-tick and zero strings matching a date pattern; assert the loading frame reserves at least one row box whose x and width equal the arrived phone's first .b-item x and width.

biggestWin: The owner's loop is honest end to end now, and that is what moved this from 7.5. Driven, not read: on owner-flight press Add a moment, type "Hair trial", press Preview — the previewed desk contains Hair trial at Sat 25 Jul, the gap note has rewritten itself from "Nothing is planned until 1 August" to "until 25 July", and Back to the plan returns eight rows with the edit intact. That was the defect most likely to lose a customer in week one and it is gone. The record room and the keepsake now list the past in full (three rows, all passing checkVisibility, no summary element at all), a cancelled item says "Not going ahead" in its own words instead of relying on a line-through, the disclosure is a 44px control with a sign on it, and every row's accessible name carries its date, its distance and whether guests can see it. The measure remains the best idea in the lab. What stands between this and 9.5 is not the direction, and it is not a rebuild: it is roughly a day and a half of composition work on the four surfaces the owner never sees. The morning is the one that matters. It holds 206 characters; it is the only guest surface that leaves what the day is out of its head, spending that slot on a sentence repeating the word above it; it labels a list of one "Happening now"; it renames the past object; and it is the only guest surface that drops the "Updated" stamp, on the one morning a guest needs to know whether the plan moved overnight. Those four are all one-line changes and together they make the morning a real title card. Beyond them sits one decision only the founder can take, and it is the one the panel circled last round and still has not closed: whether the data model carries a running order for the day. That is out of this engagement's scope, so no round here can close it. Until it is decided the morning will always be a title card — a good one once the fixes above land, but never the best screen in the product. Take the decision before Home, Notes and Tasks inherit this language, because the morning is the shape they will copy.
